idea: Plimsoll mark drawn as lettering: the circle and horizontal line with the words 'Loaded to the line. Not past it.' Samuel Plimsoll's load line became compulsory on British merchant ships under the 1876 Act; a shirt about knowing your limit, in the form of the real symbol.

The Beaufort scale as a stacked list, one word per line growing from tiny to huge: Calm, Light air, Light breeze, Gentle breeze, Moderate breeze, Fresh breeze, Strong breeze, Near gale, Gale, Strong gale, Storm, Violent storm, Hurricane force. A crescendo of real wind names, 0 to 12.

The shipping forecast sea areas set as a quiet litany, in order: Viking, North Utsire, South Utsire, Forties, Cromarty, Forth, Tyne, Dogger, Fisher, German Bight. Small caption: 'Bedtime reading for a nation.' Pure poetry of real names, for anyone who has fallen asleep to it.
'Lost 5.1 seconds in 81 days.' Large type with the small line 'Harrison's H4, to Jamaica and back, 1761-62.' The clock that solved longitude, told as one stubborn number.

'Found drifting, 4 December 1872. Nobody aboard.' Set as a ship's log entry with the line 'Mary Celeste. The cargo was fine.' (the 1,701 barrels of alcohol were largely intact). A true mystery in four plain lines.
'12 h 25 min' in huge numerals, with the line 'The sea keeps the Moon's time: high water about every twelve hours twenty-five minutes.' For people who like a fact that makes the world feel wired.

Two-line lettering: 'Starboard: the side you steered from (steerboard). Port: the side you tied up to.' Stacked, with the words mirrored left and right like the sides of a hull. Real etymology that settles every argument.
'The bitter end' in rope-style lettering, with the small line 'The last of the anchor cable, made fast to the bitts.' The idiom's actual origin, hidden in a phrase we all say.
'A knot is a knot.' Letters made of a knotted line, with the caption 'Ship speed was once counted by knots tied in a rope paid out behind the vessel.' Why we still say knots, explained in one tangle.
'By the mark, twain.' Lettered like a leadsman's call, with 'Two fathoms. Safe water.' beneath (a fathom is six feet). The origin of Mark Twain's name, as a calm shout from the bow.

A lighthouse signature in notation: 'Fl(3) W 20s' huge, with 'Three white flashes every twenty seconds. Every lighthouse has its own.' Charts really use this code; a shirt for people who like hidden systems.
'··· −−− ···' in heavy type with 'Stands for nothing. Means everything.' SOS is not an abbreviation of any phrase; it was chosen in 1906 because the Morse pattern is easy to send and recognise.
'Luke Howard named the clouds, 1802: cirrus, cumulus, stratus, nimbus.' Each word set in its own shape, wispy and heaped and flat and heavy. A pharmacist gave the sky its vocabulary.
'Same river. In Oxford it is called the Isis.' Lettering that runs in a long meander across the chest, ending with 'THAMES' at the hem. A small true oddity of the Thames that people love knowing.
'A spouting fish with a horizontal tail.' with the small credit 'Melville's definition of a whale, Moby-Dick, ch. 32. Wrong, and magnificent.' For readers who love a confident error.

'About 1,300 metres.' Large, with 'The Vasa, maiden voyage, Stockholm, 10 August 1628. Raised 1961.' The most expensive ship of its age sailed about 1,300 metres before sinking; a monument to ambition.
'Endurance. Crushed by ice 1915. Found 2022, 3,008 m down.' Set as a gravestone inscription with tidy serif capitals. Shackleton's ship, found by name still legible on the stern.
'The Sargasso Sea has no shore.' Lettering floating in loose weed-like strands, with 'A sea bounded by currents, not land.' Strange but true geography, for people who like the world's loopholes.
'Hawai'i to Tahiti, 1976. No instruments.' Set in a ring like a star compass, with 'Hokule'a, navigated by Mau Piailug.' Pure wayfinding, proof that stars, swells and birds are enough.

'Navigare necesse est, vivere non est necesse.' with the translation 'To sail is necessary; to live is not.' Attributed by Plutarch to Pompey, who sent grain ships to Rome in a storm. A motto with real weight, in classical capitals.
